Le droit à un Aïd ordinaire: The Right to an Ordinary Eid
À l’occasion de l’Aïd al-Adha, des famil: For Eid al-Adha, Muslim families in Quebec talk about how they celebrate amid a string of widely reported incidents.
La famille de Nadia et Hassan est réunie: Nadia and Hassan's family gathers in the living room for Eid breakfast, around traditional Moroccan dishes.
Ce reportage est né d’une question qui m: This report grew out of a question that followed me throughout Eid: what happens when an intimate, spiritual family celebration is at the same time cut across by the news, hateful comments and public debates about the place of Muslims in Quebec?
Pour réaliser ce texte, j’ai eu la chanc: To report this piece, I was lucky enough to be invited to Nadia and Hassan's home in Mirabel to spend part of Eid with their family. I also visited other families at home and spoke with several Muslims living in Montréal, Mirabel and the surrounding areas to gather their accounts. This subject also touches me from a personal place. I am a Moroccan Quebecer and a political science student, and I have long been interested in the ways Muslim communities are represented in public space. That position let me enter some conversations with a certain closeness, but it also required me to stay mindful of one essential thing: not to replace the words of the people I met with my own political reading.
Ce reportage ne vise pas à dresser le po: This report does not aim to paint a portrait of a community, nor to turn Eid into a symbol. Instead, it starts from ordinary moments to ask what they say about Quebec today: its political tensions, its silent fractures, but also the ways in which multiple belongings are inhabited, composed and lived.
<strong>À Trois-Rivières, une prière de: In Trois-Rivières, an Eid al-Adha prayer was enough to set off a wave of hateful comments. In Shawinigan, a few days later, a slogan about a “white Quebec” appeared in the street. With a provincial election approaching in which identity, secularism and immigration risk once again serving as political shortcuts, Eid al-Adha becomes a quiet revealer of a broader tension. In Quebec, some things Muslims do are still not seen as ordinary parts of collective life. This report tells what that does to a celebration – in living rooms, families and mosques – when it still has to pass through the gaze of others before it can simply exist.
Chez Nadia et Hassan, à Mirabel, la télé: At Nadia and Hassan's place in Mirabel, the TV is already on in the living room.
Le Canadien est en train de perdre, les: The Canadiens are losing, the kids are running from room to room and someone is looking for a plate that has vanished in the kitchen. Then Nadia looks at Hassane, absorbed in the game, and calls out: “Drop the Canadiens game. Today, play with the kids!”
La scène pourrait se dérouler dans n’imp: The scene could take place in any Quebec family on a festive evening. A game on in the background. Kids taking up too much space. A full house. Adults trying to hold the meal, the conversations and the chaos of the living room together.
Mais ce soir-là, alors que des familles: But that evening, as Muslim families celebrate Eid al-Adha in their homes, their mosques or their community halls, the celebration is also the target of hateful comments elsewhere in Quebec.
À Trois-Rivières, la tenue d’une prière: In Trois-Rivières, an Eid prayer held in a private venue provoked a wave of racist reactions and online threats. A few days later, in Shawinigan, masked demonstrators unfurled a banner bearing the words: “I remember a white Quebec.”
Entre l’intimité d’un salon et le tumult: Between the intimacy of a living room and the public uproar, a gap opens up.
Pour les familles rencontrées, l’Aïd n’e: For the families I met, Eid is not first of all a social issue. It is a day of reunion, transmission and love. Yet the news always ends up coming into the home, one way or another. Through a notification. Through a video. In a question asked at school. In the eyes of a child who realizes all too quickly that their celebration can become, for others, a problem.
Nadia est famille d’accueil depuis plusi: Nadia has been a foster parent for several years. In her home, she often sees how much children pick up on what adults think they are hiding from them. “Kids absorb everything,” she says. “Even when you think they're not listening, they're listening.”
Ce qu’ils entendent ne vient pas seuleme: What they hear doesn't come only from their parents. It also comes from school, social media, conversations caught in passing. Her 12-year-old son recently told her about videos that mock Muslims. They laugh at the sacrifice of the sheep. They turn a religious practice into a cheap joke. They present Eid as something strange, almost suspect.
Le ton se veut parfois humoristique. Mai: The tone is sometimes meant to be humorous. But for a child watching, the effect is no joke. He understands that what is normal at home can become material for mockery once he steps outside.
Sa fille, elle, est revenue de l’école a: Her daughter came home from school with a different question. A classmate had called Eid weird. She wanted to understand why. “Before, kids only thought about the gifts and their cousins,” Nadia says. “Now they ask questions a child shouldn't even have to ask themselves.”
C’est peut-être ainsi que l’actualité en: Perhaps this is how the news enters homes most deeply. Not always through big headlines, but through a sentence brought back from the schoolyard. Through a word that forces a parent to explain too early what they would have liked to keep outside.
Nadia ne veut pas faire de l’Aïd une jou: Nadia doesn't want to turn Eid into a day of justification. She doesn't want to spend this celebration correcting other people's gaze. She wants the kids to play. To laugh. To keep simple memories of this day.
Mais dans un climat où les pratiques mus: But in a climate where Muslim practices regularly return to public space as controversy, protecting that simplicity already takes effort.
Cette année, le contexte a donné une dim: This year, the context gave this tension a particular dimension.
À Trois-Rivières, des images d’une prièr: In Trois-Rivières, images of an Eid prayer held in a private venue were widely shared online. The post triggered a series of hateful and racist comments, to the point that the Canadian Muslim Forum asked authorities to act.
Quelques semaines plus tôt, à Gatineau,: A few weeks earlier, in Gatineau, a man had been arrested after sending death threats to the imam and worshippers of the Aylmer mosque. The incident revived fears in several communities deeply marked by the 2017 attack on the Quebec City mosque.
Aux États-Unis, l’attaque contre l’Islam: In the United States, the attack on the Islamic Center of San Diego, in which three worshippers were killed, also circulated on news feeds. Even from afar, this kind of violence reaches families by the same routes as everything else: WhatsApp groups, video clips, conversations among loved ones, phone alerts.
Pris séparément, ces événements ne racon: Taken separately, these events do not tell the story of the families I met. But their accumulation creates a certain climate.
Un climat où une fête familiale peut êtr: A climate in which a family celebration can be lived as a celebration in a living room and discussed elsewhere as a threat, an anomaly or one sign too many.
Pour Nicerine et sa famille, la déconnex: For Nicerine and her family, the disconnection begins even before Eid.
Depuis quelques années, elle consacre le: For the past few years, she has devoted the days leading up to the celebration to fasting. In Muslim tradition, the first days of the month of Dhul-Hijja, especially the day of Arafat, are times of reflection. Many believers fast on this occasion, pray more and try to slow down.
Pour Nicerine, ce ralentissement a aussi: For Nicerine, this slowing down also has a very current resonance. “It helps me refocus,” she explains. “I try to be less on my phone, less in the news. It's a good time to refocus on my spirituality and my family.”
Elle rit doucement avant d’ajouter : « S: She laughs softly before adding: “Otherwise, we go crazy.” Her sentence says something about an era in which every crisis demands a piece of our attention. You have to watch. React. Understand. Share. Take a position. And start over.
Mais pour plusieurs familles musulmanes,: But for many Muslim families, this exhaustion has an extra layer. It's not only the world's crises that come into the home. It's also seeing their own religion, their holidays, their prayers or their places of worship constantly return to the news as objects of debate.
Pour Nicerine, ralentir signifie choisir: For Nicerine, slowing down means choosing what deserves to be protected before going back into the noise.
Connu sous le pseudonyme de Malik Shabaz: Known by the pseudonym Malik Shabazz, Malik is a political content creator on TikTok in Montréal. A single father of a nine-year-old girl, his days consist of dissecting the news, analyzing power dynamics and talking about Gaza, Iran, the United States – everything that's going wrong.
Alors, quand il parle de l’Aïd, sa voix: So when he talks about Eid, his voice changes. It slows down. “We're constantly bombarded with bad news; it feels good to detach from that,” he says.
Sa famille est « très politisée », dit-i: His family is “very politicized,” he says. The news takes up “more and more space in our discussions.” His daughter, who is nine, is starting to hear things on TikTok: talk about war, hateful remarks that exclude her, violent shortcuts about Islam and immigration. Images and words she shouldn't have known so early.
Alors l’Aïd, pour Malik, n’est pas une é: So for Malik, Eid is not an escape. It is a counter-space, as he puts it. “It's not about ignoring what's happening in the world,” he clarifies. “It's about reminding my daughter that, despite the chaos, you still have family. You still have moments of happiness. You still have religion. You still have stability, right?”
Il insiste sur ce <em>right</em>, comme: He stresses that right, as if to make sure he's been understood. It isn't denial. It's a declaration of continuity. A way of saying: the world may be on fire, but we hold on.
« Je pense que tous les parents cherchen: “I think all parents are looking for a bit of that right now, regardless of religion.”
Ce qu’il décrit, c’est un glissement sil: What he describes is a silent shift that many immigrant families experience. The celebration becomes an emotional necessity. A need to remind themselves that before being political subjects, before being scrutinized, questioned, mocked on TikTok, they are first a family.
« On reste profondément attachés au Québ: “We remain deeply attached to Quebec, to our life here,” he says. “But we're going to keep certain family traditions that remind us where we come from.”
À Montréal, Myriam observe cette transfo: In Montréal, Myriam notices this transformation in a more discreet detail: the doors of mosques.
Professeure de langue arabe et d’études: A teacher of Arabic and Quranic studies, and a dedicated volunteer in Montréal mosques, she arrived in Quebec more than 20 years ago. She remembers a time when mosques were more accessible, almost part of the ordinary rhythm of the day.
« Avant, les mosquées étaient ouvertes t: “Before, mosques were open all day,” she explains. “I'd be out shopping, I'd hear the call to prayer, so I'd step into the nearest mosque for a few minutes before heading back to my shopping. Now, often, the doors are closed. You have to ring the bell. Sometimes you need a code to get in. These security measures have been strengthened since 2017.”
Elle ne raconte pas cela avec colère. Pl: She doesn't say this with anger. Rather with lucidity. As if vigilance had become a habit.
Là aussi, l’actualité laisse une trace c: Here too, the news leaves a concrete trace. Not only in speeches, but in how space is organized: locked doors, codes, stricter hours, a caution built into daily life.
Pourtant, Myriam insiste sur ce qui deme: Yet Myriam insists on what remains.
Les familles se réunissent encore. Les e: Families still gather. Children learn Arabic to talk with their grandparents. Women still organize get-togethers after the holiday. People cook. They laugh. They carry on. “We carry on anyway,” she says simply.
<strong>Le droit de ne pas être une ques: The right not to be a question
À Trois-Rivières, la prière de l'Aïd org: In Trois-Rivières, the Eid prayer held on May 27 at the racetrack by the Minhaj-as-Sunna mosque had brought together about 200 people in a private, authorized venue. After images were shared online, some comments referred to Alexandre Bissonnette, the perpetrator of the attack on the Grande Mosquée de Québec, while others spoke of setting fire to the gathering. Mayor Jean François Aubin said he was deeply shocked by these unacceptable remarks, noting that the event was legal and had disturbed no one nearby.
Le lendemain, le Forum musulman canadien: The next day, the Canadian Muslim Forum asked authorities to take these messages seriously and to launch an investigation. The organization said these comments could not be treated as mere online excesses, stressing that they were part of a collective memory still marked by the anti-Muslim violence that has already occurred in Quebec.
À l'Assemblée nationale, les réactions n: At the National Assembly, reactions were swift. On June 2, 2026, all parties unanimously voted for a Québec solidaire motion condemning racism and supremacist ideologies. Premier Christine Fréchette said she was “deeply shocked” by the Shawinigan gathering. “Such remarks are unacceptable and have no place in our society,” she said. Sol Zanetti, co-spokesperson for Québec solidaire, did not stop at condemnation: “We also have to act,” he said, pointing to the government's inaction on racial profiling. A rare political front. It remains to be seen, for the families I met in Mirabel and Montréal, how these words will translate concretely into their daily lives.
